findings.title: limitFunction drops every caller argument
findings.cause: The returned wrapper ignores its own arguments and calls the wrapped function with no arguments: `return () => limit(() => function_());`.
findings.impact: The named export is unusable for the documented and typed use case where the limited function accepts inputs, for example `limitedFetchUrl(url)`. All inputs become `undefined` at runtime.
evidence: index.js:121-125 returns a zero-argument wrapper and calls `function_()` without forwarding `...arguments_`.
readme.md:111-130 documents `limitFunction(fn, options)` and shows callers invoking the limited function repeatedly.
recipes.md:161-163 shows `urls.map(url => limitedFetchUrl(url))`, which requires argument forwarding.
index.d.ts:133-136 types `limitFunction` as returning `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: After installing dependencies, `node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async value => value, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(JSON.stringify({limitFunctionArgument: String(await limited('sentinel'))}));"` printed `{"limitFunctionArgument":"undefined"}`.

findings.title: limit.map omits indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper wrapper checks `Array.isArray(iterable)` and passes `undefined` as the index for any other iterable.
findings.impact: The public `limit.map` contract says the mapper receives both value and index. Sets, generators, and array iterators now receive `undefined` for the second argument, breaking callers that rely on stable indexing.
evidence: index.js:106-114 computes `iterableIsArray` and passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined` to the mapper.
readme.md:78-84 says the mapper receives the item value and its index and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`.
index.d.ts:40-43 types the mapper as `(input: Input, index: number)` for every iterable.
test.js:239-254 covers Set and array iterator values but does not assert the index argument.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused probe: `await pLimit(1).map(new Set(['a', 'b']), async (value, index) => `${value}:${String(index)}`)` produced `["a:undefined","b:undefined"]`.

findings.title: Options-object default now rejects queued promises on clearQueue
findings.cause: Destructuring changed the options-object default from `rejectOnClear = false` to `rejectOnClear = true`.
findings.impact: `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` no longer matches the documented default. Calling `clearQueue()` unexpectedly rejects pending promises with `AbortError`, which can turn cleanup paths into user-visible failures.
evidence: index.js:4-8 initializes `rejectOnClear` to false but then destructures options with `rejectOnClear = true`.
readme.md:46-52 documents `rejectOnClear` as `Default: false`.
index.d.ts:99-106 documents `rejectOnClear?: boolean` as defaulting to false.
test.js:184-194 covers `clearQueue()` only for numeric `pLimit(1)`, while test.js:199-215 covers explicit `{rejectOnClear: true}`; no test covers `{concurrency: 1}` with omitted `rejectOnClear`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused probe using `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const pending = limit(() => 'should-not-run'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue();` observed `defaultRejectOnClearStatus: "rejected:AbortError"` for the pending promise.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The runtime type check only runs when `rejectOnClear` is truthy: `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`.
findings.impact: Invalid API inputs such as `0`, `''`, or `null` are silently accepted and treated like false, contrary to the documented boolean contract. This hides configuration mistakes and makes runtime validation inconsistent.
evidence: index.js:12-14 skips validation for falsy non-boolean values.
readme.md:46-49 documents `rejectOnClear` as type `boolean`.
index.d.ts:99-106 types `rejectOnClear?: boolean`.
index.test-d.ts:29 rejects a string at type level, but there is no runtime test for falsy non-booleans.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused probe called `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value})` for `0`, `''`, and `null`; all were accepted instead of throwing `TypeError`.

findings.title: Infinity is rejected as a concurrency value
findings.cause: The validator now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the previous `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance.
findings.impact: Callers can no longer opt into an effectively unlimited limiter with `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`, despite the public contract describing a number with minimum 1 and no finite maximum. This is a breaking edge-case regression.
evidence: index.js:127-130 accepts only positive integers.
git diff -- index.js shows the committed baseline accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`.
readme.md:37-44 documents `concurrency` as type `number | object` with minimum 1 and does not document a finite upper bound.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused probe `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` produced `threw:TypeError:Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up`.

findings.title: The package test script fails before behavioral tests complete
findings.cause: The `map` property block is over-indented relative to the surrounding descriptor object.
findings.impact: `npm test` exits non-zero at the `xo` step, so CI/release validation fails even though `ava` and `tsd` pass when run separately.
evidence: index.js:105-115 has the over-indented `map` descriptor block.
package.json:22-24 defines `test` as `xo && ava && tsd`.
`npm test` reported XO `@stylistic/indent` errors at index.js:105-115.
findings.reproduction_or_test: `npm test` exited with code 1 and reported 11 indentation errors in index.js:105-115. Separate `npx ava` ran 21 passing tests and `npx tsd` exited 0.
